paragraphs.greek: Μετὰ τὰς μάχας οἱ ἐν τῷ Πειραιεῖ καὶ οἱ ἐν τῷ ἄστει περὶ εἰρήνης βουλεύονται. οὐ γὰρ ἀρκεῖ τὰ ὅπλα θεῖναι· δεῖ καὶ τρόπον εὑρεῖν τοῦ μετ᾽ ἀλλήλων ζῆν. οἱ μὲν νικῶντες τοὺς φίλους τοὺς ἀπολομένους μνημονεύουσιν, οἱ δὲ ἄλλοι τὴν τιμωρίαν φοβοῦνται. ἡ πόλις τὴν μὲν χώραν μίαν ἔχει, τὰς δὲ γνώμας διῃρημένας.

Σπονδαὶ οὖν γίγνονται, καὶ ἕκαστοι πρὸς τὰ ἑαυτῶν ἐπανέρχονται. ἐν δὲ ταῖς σπονδαῖς διαφορὰ γίνεται περὶ τῶν Τριάκοντα καὶ τῶν Ἕνδεκα καὶ τῶν ἐν Πειραιεῖ δέκα ἀρξάντων. τούτους οὐ τῷ αὐτῷ τρόπῳ περιλαμβάνει ἡ συμφωνία. τοῖς δὲ φοβουμένοις ἐξὸν ἦν εἰς Ἐλευσῖνα ἀπιέναι. τὴν διάκρισιν ταύτην μὴ παραλείπωμεν, ὅταν περὶ τῆς εἰρήνης λέγωμεν.

Οἱ ἐκ τοῦ Πειραιῶς ἀνελθόντες εἰς τὴν ἀκρόπολιν θύουσι τῇ Ἀθηνᾷ. ἔπειτα ἡ κοινὴ πολιτεία πάλιν καθίσταται. ὕστερον δὲ καὶ περὶ Ἐλευσῖνος νέα πράγματα γίγνεται, καὶ οὐχ ἅπαντα ἄνευ βίας τελεῖται. τέλος δὲ ὀμνύουσι μὴ μνησικακήσειν. ὁ Ξενοφῶν λέγει ὅτι οἱ πολῖται τοῖς ὅρκοις ἐμμένουσιν ἐν τῷ χρόνῳ περὶ οὗ γράφει.

paragraphs.greek: Νῦν ἐν τῷ μαθήματι τρεῖς προτάσεις συγκρίνομεν. ἐὰν τοῖς ὅρκοις ἐμμένωμεν, πιστότεροι ἐσόμεθα. εἰ τοῖς ὅρκοις ἐμμένοιμεν, πιστότεροι ἂν εἴημεν. εἰ τοῖς ὅρκοις ἐνεμείναμεν, πιστότεροι ἂν ἐγενόμεθα. ἡ πρώτη πρότασις μέλλον σαφέστερον προσδοκᾷ, ἡ δὲ δευτέρα δυνατὸν ἡπιώτερον τίθησιν, ἡ δὲ τρίτη περὶ πράγματος παρελθόντος παρὰ τὰ γενόμενα λέγει.

Οὐ μόνον δὲ δυνατὰ ἀλλὰ καὶ ἀναγκαῖα σκοποῦμεν. τοὺς ὅρκους φυλακτέον ἐστίν· τὰς αἰτίας ἐξεταστέον, οὐ τοὺς ἀνθρώπους ἄνευ κρίσεως κολαστέον. δέον γὰρ κοινῇ ζῆν, οὐ χρήσιμον ἀεὶ τὸ παλαιὸν μῖσος αὔξειν. ὁ μὲν τὸ σῶμα ἰσχυρός, ὁ δὲ τὴν γνώμην πιστὸς ἔστω. οὐ πᾶσα δύναμις τὴν αὐτὴν ὠφέλειαν παρέχει.

Ὁ τῆς εἰρήνης λόγος οὐ κελεύει πάντα τὰ κακὰ ἀγαθὰ νομίζειν. ζητεῖ πῶς οἱ διαφερόμενοι τὴν αὐτὴν πόλιν οἰκήσουσιν. ἐὰν τὴν ἀσφάλειαν μόνον τοῖς φίλοις παρέχωμεν, τί ποιήσουσιν οἱ ἄλλοι; εἰ δὲ πάντας ὑπόπτους νομίζομεν, πῶς κοινὰ ἔργα πράττομεν; ταῦτα ἐρωτῶντες τὰς μὲν ἡμετέρας προτάσεις γράφομεν, τὰ δὲ ἐν τῇ διηγήσει γενόμενα χωρὶς ἐξετάζομεν.

reading.translation:
After the battles, those in Piraeus and those in the city deliberate about peace. It is not enough to lay down arms; they must also find a way to live with one another. The victors remember their friends who died, while the others fear punishment. The city has one territory but divided opinions.

An agreement is therefore made, and each party returns to its own property. The terms distinguish the Thirty, the Eleven, and the ten who had ruled in Piraeus. The agreement does not include them in the same way. Those who were afraid were permitted to depart to Eleusis. Let us not omit this distinction when speaking about peace.

Those from Piraeus go up to the Acropolis and sacrifice to Athena. The common constitution is then restored. Later new events occur concerning Eleusis, and not everything is accomplished without violence. Finally they swear not to recall past wrongs against one another. Xenophon says that the citizens abide by their oaths in the period about which he writes.

Now in the lesson we compare three proposals. If we abide by our oaths, we shall be more trustworthy. If we were to abide by our oaths, we would be more trustworthy. If we had abided by our oaths, we would have been more trustworthy. The first expects a more definite future, the second presents a possibility more tentatively, and the third speaks counterfactually about a past event.

We consider not only possibilities but also necessities. We must keep the oaths; we must examine accusations, not punish people without judgment. Since it is necessary to live together, it is not useful constantly to increase old hatred. Let one be strong in body and another trustworthy in judgment. Not every kind of strength provides the same benefit.

The argument for peace does not command us to regard every wrong as good. It asks how those who disagree will inhabit the same city. If we provide safety only for friends, what will the others do? If we consider everyone suspect, how do we undertake common tasks? In asking these questions we write our own proposals, while separately examining what happened in the narrative.

objectives: Conditional sentences: build the assigned system, including open conditions, future more vivid and less vivid, general conditions, and contrary-to-fact conditions.
Identify protasis and apodosis, tense/mood, negation, and ἄν; interpret the speaker’s stance before naming the category.

sections.title: 1. Conditions: open and future more vivid
body: A conditional sentence has a protasis, the if-clause, and an apodosis, its consequence. An open condition uses εἰ with indicative and presents an assumption without marking it as contrary to fact: εἰ τοῦτο ποιεῖ, ἀδικεῖ. The tense can be present or past as the context requires.

A future more vivid condition uses ἐάν with subjunctive, normally followed by a future indicative or equivalent consequence: ἐὰν ἐμμείνωμεν, πιστοὶ ἐσόμεθα. It presents a future contingency relatively directly, not as a guarantee that it will occur. Negative protasis normally uses μή; the apodosis follows the negation appropriate to its own construction.

sections.title: 2. Future less vivid and general conditions
body: Future less vivid commonly uses εἰ with optative and an apodosis with optative plus ἄν: εἰ ἐμμένοιμεν, πιστοὶ ἂν εἴημεν. “If we were to abide, we would be trustworthy” presents a more tentative future possibility. It does not by itself say that we failed in the past.

Present general uses ἐάν + subjunctive and present indicative: whenever a citizen keeps an oath, trust grows. Past general uses εἰ + optative and imperfect indicative, without potential ἄν in the ordinary apodosis. These generalize across repeated occasions. Distinguish the time of the generalization from the stem aspect of the subordinate verb.

sections.title: 3. Contrary-to-fact conditions
body: A contrary-to-fact condition normally has εἰ with a past indicative, and a past indicative with ἄν in the consequence. The imperfect often marks a present unreal situation: εἰ δίκαιος ἦν, οὐκ ἂν ἠδίκει, “If he were just, he would not be doing wrong.” The aorist commonly marks a past unreal action.

Compare εἰ ἔμεινεν, ἐσώθη with εἰ ἔμεινεν, ἐσώθη ἄν: the first is an open past condition; the second, in its normal reading, “If he had stayed, he would have been saved.” Mixed time relations are possible. Decide what time each clause describes before assigning a label.

sections.title: 4. Adverbial accusative and respect
body: An accusative can measure extent in space or time without being a direct object: πολὺν χρόνον ἔμειναν, “They stayed a long time.” Other accusatives function adverbially. Identify the verb’s ordinary argument pattern before calling every accusative an object.

The accusative of respect limits the claim made by an adjective or verb: ἰσχυρὸς τὸ σῶμα, “strong in body.” It does not say that the body is an object being acted upon. Compare τὴν γνώμην πιστός, “trustworthy in judgment,” and distinguish this from an agreeing nominative description of the person.

sections.title: 5. Accusative absolute
body: An absolute construction supplies a circumstance without being a normal argument of the main clause. Impersonal participles often form an accusative absolute: ἐξόν, “it being permitted”; δέον, “it being necessary”; δυνατόν/ἀδύνατον ὄν, “it being possible/impossible.” An infinitive can complete the expression.

Compare ἐξὸν ἀπιέναι, ἔμεινεν, “Although it was possible to leave, he stayed.” The concessive force comes from context, not a special ending. The familiar genitive absolute commonly has a noun or pronoun plus agreeing participle; the impersonal accusative absolute is usually neuter singular.

sections.title: 6. Necessity with -τέος
body: Verbal adjectives in -τέος express what must be done. In a personal construction the adjective agrees with the thing requiring action: ὁ νόμος φυλακτέος ἐστίν, “The law must be kept.” A dative can identify the responsible agent: ἡμῖν, “by us.”

In an impersonal construction neuter -τέον, often with ἐστί, expresses “one must.” An active verb can retain its ordinary object: ἡμῖν τὸν νόμον φυλακτέον, “We must keep the law.” Do not confuse this necessity adjective with -τός, which can express a state or possibility. In both constructions identify who must act and what action is required.

sections.title: Meet Xenophon’s Hellenica
body: Follow Book 2, chapter 4 beyond the military return to Athens. Settlement, exceptions, the Eleusis episode, and adherence to oaths form a sequence with achievements and tensions. The text gives a political account of restored coexistence, not a claim that past harm never happened. Keep the actual terms separate from the conditional proposals you will compose in class.

The seven books cover Greek affairs from 411 to 362 BCE, beginning where Thucydides’ unfinished history breaks off. They follow Athens’ defeat in the Peloponnesian War, oligarchy and democratic restoration, Spartan ascendancy, shifting alliances, and the rise of Thebes. The closing battle at Mantinea leaves uncertainty rather than a simple declaration that one city has permanently won.

Xenophon organizes political and military events through commanders, assemblies, negotiations, speeches, and judgments about conduct. His attention is selective, and his experience and sympathies shape the narrative. Ask what a speech tries to accomplish, whose actions receive explanation, and what a compressed transition leaves unclear. A historian’s ordering of events can be as significant as an explicit verdict.

Reading invitation: start with Book 2, chapter 3, on the Thirty, then follow chapter 4 through resistance and restoration. Compare the settlement with the later Eleusis episode instead of stopping at the hopeful return to Athens. Our module’s question has grown from control of appetite to restraint in civic life: what practices let former enemies inhabit one city? Read the complete work as a sequence of difficult choices, not a storehouse of uncomplicated moral examples.
Follow the sequence before evaluating the settlement as a whole.

sections.title: Reconciliation with terms
body: Hellenica 2.4 describes the settlement after civil conflict, the return of those from Piraeus, and the restoration of civic life. The agreement has named exceptions and provisions; it is not an undifferentiated declaration that all past acts no longer matter. Read the treatment of the Thirty, the Eleven, and the ten who ruled in Piraeus carefully.

People who feared remaining in the city could withdraw to Eleusis under the terms described. Later events involving Eleusis complicate a simple story of peaceful closure. Xenophon’s account should be followed beyond the triumphant return before drawing conclusions about reconciliation.

sections.title: The oath and its limits
body: The pledge not to recall past wrongs against one another is a political commitment that helps former opponents inhabit a common civic order. It does not mean that injuries were unreal, that everyone forgot them, or that every participant was equally responsible. The distinction between memory and retaliatory action is central.

Xenophon praises adherence to the oaths in the period he describes. Treat this as his assessment of a civic achievement, with a temporal scope. Do not turn it into a claim that Athens never again experienced conflict or injustice.

sections.title: Draft a settlement
body: Write three provisions addressing safety, accountability, and return. For each, state what happens if it is kept or broken. Label your document a modern classroom proposal. Compare its terms with the actual source, noting both an agreement and a difference.

Translate the source-based opening separately from the course’s conditional models. Then explain how moving from future more vivid to future less vivid changes the speaker’s stance. Complete the necessity and accusative exercises before translating the closing proposal without interruption.
